title: The Ahluwalia misl
hook: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia's misl, later the state of Kapurthala

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhangi misl, with its great gun and its two cities. Your line was strong, for a time. What strength did you hand on? Today, a band that was known for one man. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

Two hats. That's the problem today's chief had. You've met Jassa Singh Ahluwalia on this path already: the boy who sang kirtan, the young rider Nawab Kapur Singh trained, the man the Khalsa called Sultan-ul-Qaum. Today, look at him from a different side. He had his own band, with its own riders and villages to look after. And he was also the one the chiefs looked to when all the bands rode together. Lead your own people, and lead everyone. Today: the Ahluwalia misl.
screen: `TWO HATS.` → `HIS OWN BAND.` → `AND THE WHOLE DAL KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Four pieces. The first is the name. Tradition says Jassa Singh's family came from a village called Ahlu, near Lahore, and his band took its name from it: Ahluwalia, the ones from Ahlu. The second piece is the first hat. As chief of his own misl, he had riders who had chosen to ride with him and villages that looked to his band for protection. That's the ordinary work of a sardar: keep your people fed, safe and together. The third piece is the second hat. Tradition says that when the bands gathered at Amritsar and rode as the Dal Khalsa, the chiefs put Jassa Singh at the head. Think about what that asks of a man. When the spoils are shared, does his own band get the best? When there's a hard job, does it go to someone else's riders? In the way Sikh histories tell it, the chiefs of other bands trusted him, and that trust is the whole point. A leader of everyone can't lead only for his own. The fourth piece is what the band became. Long after the riding years, the lands of the Ahluwalia misl became the state of Kapurthala, ruled by chiefs who carried the Ahluwalia name. The band outlasted the age of bands. Other misls on this path are remembered for a fort, a flag, a river or a fight. This one is remembered because of who led it, and because the man who led it was trusted beyond it. It's the leader's misl.
screen: `AHLUWALIA: THE ONES FROM AHLU.` · `CHIEF OF HIS OWN BAND.` · `AT THE HEAD OF THE DAL KHALSA.` · `HIS LANDS BECAME KAPURTHALA.` · then, large: `THE LEADER'S MISL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a leader. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who has led you well: a coach, a manager, a teacher, an older cousin. Not someone famous, someone whose leading you felt up close. Notice whether they were fair to people who weren't their own. Notice what they did that made you trust them. On each breath, let yourself be thankful for one thing they did. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

The Ahluwalia misl. Jassa Singh's band from Ahlu, whose lands became Kapurthala. This week: chardi kala in the century, the women who kept the homes, what the century teaches, the hard century's close, the misl, the Bhangis, and the Ahluwalias. Today's word.
Your line: the leader's misl. Today, tell one person who led you well what they did right. Leaders rarely hear it. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Jassa Singh Ahluwalia in Sikh histories and gurdwara talks as a leader of the Dal Khalsa, and the Ahluwalia name lives on in families and in the town of Kapurthala.

fork.setup: you're Jassa Singh, at the head of the Dal Khalsa. the spoils of a campaign are being shared among the bands. your own riders are watching. what do you do?
options: give your own band the best share.
share fairly, so the other chiefs keep trusting you.
send it all to Amritsar and let no band share.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Ahluwalia misl was one band among many.
what it means: it was Jassa Singh's band, and he wore two hats: its chief, and head of the whole Dal Khalsa.
what a scholar hears: the band outlasted the age of bands; its lands became the state of Kapurthala.
